title: How the estimate works
text: The colored curves in the VLOS estimator answer one question for every altitude: how far away, horizontally, can the drone be before it looks smaller than a chosen visual-acuity threshold?
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

title: How the estimate works
text:
Geometry
Picture the pilot and the drone from the side. The pilot’s eye is at the origin. The drone’s center is a horizontal distance \(d\) away and at altitude \(a\) above the eye. The drone’s side profile is treated as a rectangle \(w\) wide and \(h\) tall.
The model measures the angle \(\theta\) that the rectangle’s diagonal subtends at the eye, from the near top corner \(A\) to the far bottom corner \(B\):
\[
A = \left(d - \tfrac{w}{2},\; a + \tfrac{h}{2}\right), \qquad
B = \left(d + \tfrac{w}{2},\; a - \tfrac{h}{2}\right)
\]
The angle between two vectors satisfies \(\tan\theta = |A \times B| \,/\, (A \cdot B)\). Expanding both terms gives
\[
\tan\theta = \frac{w\,a + h\,d}{d^2 + a^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}\left(w^2 + h^2\right)}
\]
The numerator is the drone’s extent perpendicular to the line of sight. The denominator is roughly the squared distance to the drone. At long range this reduces to the familiar small-angle rule: apparent size ≈ projected size ÷ distance.
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

title: How the estimate works
text:
Solving for the maximum distance
Let \(\theta_{\min}\) be the acuity threshold and \(t = \tan\theta_{\min}\). The drone is at or above the threshold wherever
\[
t\,d^2 - h\,d + c \le 0, \qquad c = t\left(a^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}(w^2 + h^2)\right) - w\,a
\]
This is a quadratic in \(d\), so the farthest horizontal distance at which the drone still meets the threshold is its larger root:
\[
d_{\max} = \frac{h + \sqrt{h^2 - 4\,t\,c}}{2t}
\]
If the discriminant \(h^2 - 4tc\) is negative, the drone is below the threshold at every horizontal distance at that altitude, even directly overhead. The plot leaves a gap there instead of drawing a line.






NoteWhy a closed form instead of a search?





An earlier version stepped outward 2 ft at a time until the angle dropped below the threshold. That took roughly 200 ms per keystroke for a typical drone, could freeze the browser for very large inputs, and reported 2 ft when the drone was never visible. The closed form gives the same answer (checked to within floating-point error against a bisection search) in a fraction of a millisecond.
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

Acuity thresholds
Visual acuity is measured as the smallest angle, in arcminutes (′), that the eye can resolve. One arcminute is 1/60 of a degree.

The 1′ curve is a resolution limit, not a detection limit. A dark, high-contrast object against a bright sky can sometimes be noticed at a smaller angle, while a low-contrast object may not be noticed at a much larger one.

title: How the estimate works
section: Why the x-axis is horizontal distance
text:
Why the x-axis is horizontal distance
Pilots plan flights on a map, so the plot shows ground distance from the pilot. The straight-line (slant) distance is always longer: \(\sqrt{d^2 + a^2}\). This matters when comparing against EASA’s formula, which is defined as a straight-line distance. See The EASA formula.

title: Experiment
text: The VLOS estimator predicts how far away a drone stays visible, based on its angular size: how large it appears to the observer. These trials test that prediction directly.
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

title: Experiment

Method

Drones
Four drones were flown, ranging from a 249 g quadcopter to a fixed-wing mapping aircraft. Dimensions were measured on each aircraft.

Flights and observers
The multirotor trials were flown between June 11 and June 20, 2025. 8 observers took part, with experience ranging from beginner to experienced pilot. Several observers watched the same flights at the same time, giving 32 observer sessions in total. Each observer recorded whether they could see the drone, and those records were matched to the drone’s flight log by time.


Angular size
Each observation’s angular size was computed from the drone’s horizontal distance and altitude relative to the observer, using the same model as the estimator. The model treats the drone as seen from the side, so it is a conservative measure: it describes a drone flying straight toward or away from the observer. See How the estimate works.


Measurement accuracy
Angular size depends on distance, so errors matter in proportion to how far away the drone is: a distance error of ΔR changes the angle by about ΔR ÷ R.
GPS positions from consumer drones and phones are typically accurate to a few meters, which is small compared with the hundreds of feet at which drones were lost.
Timing is the larger risk. Devices were synchronized manually before each flight and checked against https://www.time.gov/. A 3-second error at 25 ft/s shifts the drone’s position by up to 75 ft. Observers typically lost sight of the drone about 830 ft away, so that error would change the angle by roughly 9%, and only if the drone was flying straight toward or away from the observer.

text: A set of interactive tools to support pre-flight planning and risk assessment. These are aids for thinking through a mission systematically — they don’t replace a pilot’s judgment or your organization’s own safety procedures and regulatory compliance requirements.

title: Decision Support Tools
text:
UC Drones Toolset

UC Mission Risk Checker — Rate pilot, aircraft, location, flight plan, weather, ground crew, and organizational readiness to visualize an overall mission risk profile before flying.
Visual Line of Sight Estimator — Estimates the maximum distance at which a given drone model remains visible to the naked eye, based on aircraft size and standard visual acuity thresholds.
Standoff Distance for Operations over Buildings — Calculates the minimum safe horizontal distance needed to maintain line of sight on a drone flying above a building, based on building height, length, and flight altitude.

title: Reading Remote ID
text: One purpose of Remote ID is to give law enforcement and security personnel information for identifying aircraft. Broadcasts are transmitted by one of four methods: Bluetooth 4 Legacy Advertising, Bluetooth 5 Long Range Advertising, Wi-Fi Neighbor Awareness Network (NAN), or Wi-Fi Beacon. The method used determines which devices can detect a given broadcast.

title: Reading Remote ID
text:
Mobile Devices
Android devices can receive Remote ID messages over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.






Warning



iOS devices are currently only able to read RemoteID messages over Bluetooth.


Available apps:

OpenDroneID, available on Android
Drone Scanner, available on Android and iOS


Android Wi-Fi Scan Throttling
Android 8.0 and later limit the frequency of Wi-Fi scans, which prevents reliable detection of Wi-Fi broadcasts. To disable throttling, enable Developer options (Settings, About phone, tap Build number seven times), then turn off “Wi-Fi scan throttling” under the Networking category. Menu names vary by device manufacturer.

title: FCC Regulations
text:
In an unprecedented move, on December 22, 2025, the FCC declared that UAS and UAS critical component parts that are produced in foreign countries pose unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States and to the safety and security of U.S. persons, and should be included on the FCC’s Covered List.

FCC Press Release and Fact Sheet here
The updated FCC Covered List can be found here







ImportantRestrictions on foreign-made drones



New foreign-made drones are prohibited from receiving FCC authorization and are therefore prohibited from being imported for use or sale in the U.S. This update to the Covered List does not prohibit the import, sale, or use of any existing device models the FCC previously authorized.


This FCC action goes above and beyond the initial Section 1709 review that previously only targeted DJI and Autel. The final rule covers all foreign drones and components - not just those made in China, but all foreign countries including Canada, Switzerland, UK, and Germany. In addition, the updated definition for critical components now includes batteries and motors, in addition to the usual autopilots, controllers, and cameras.
In the months following, the FCC continued to make significant changes and announcements. We have moved this information and the relevant definitions to this new page to help people keep track.






Note



The FCC has opened a handful of opportunities for the public to comment on their proposals. To date, the FCC’s response to the public on this matter and others have been to state “We disagree with the commenters.”




The current list of FCC exemptions (Aug 18, 2026)

UAS and UAS components on the DoD Blue List are allowed to receive updates and introduce new components for FCC authorization until January 1, 2028
UAS and UAS components that qualify as `domestic end products’ under the Buy American Standard will continue to be eligible for FCC authorizations until January 1, 2028.
Specific devices that have been granted a Conditional Approval by DoD or DHS
Foreign-produces ‘toy drones’ and ‘toy drones’ that contain foreign-produced components

Full list of Conditional Approvals
Update - Jan 21, 2026
The FCC has issued a waiver of prohibitions on certain Class 1 permissive changes to covered UAS and UAS critical components until January 1, 2027. This means that drones with already existing FCC approval may continue to receive certain software and firmware updates at least until then. The FCC remarks that they would re-evaluate prior to Jan 1, 2027 on whether to extend the waiver further.
So for now, foreign-made drones can continue to issue updates, but may not at some point in the future.





DJI has taken a number of actions to respond and get unbanned. You can follow along their progress in this formal docket. Link



The FCC recently announced that they were proposing to remove FCC authorization to sell or market what they deem to be ‘military’ drones. Military drones in their definition includes drones over 55 lbs, drones with a LIDAR unit, and drones with a thermal imager. While certain DJI drones have been grandfathered in with existing FCC authorizations, this would remove them from being able to be sold in the US. The proposal would not ban their use - yet.
As an example, the DJI Matrice 4E received its FCC authorization before the ban, but if this new proposal is enacted, the FCC would remove its authorization to be sold in the US.
Comments to the FCC are due Sept 2, 2026

title: Cybersecurity
text: The use of an unmanned aircraft system (UAS) designed, manufactured, or supplied by foreign companies could create increased cybersecurity risks and opportunities for network exploitation and collection by foreign threat actors.

title: Cybersecurity
Cybersecurity
text:
Mitigation Strategies
Here are a couple of suggestions to reduce the potential data risks and vulnerabilities associated with UAS use and mitigate the loss of sensitive information.

During initial UAS activation, use a department or lab name, email address, and password to reduce a UAS manufacturer’s ability to track the owner/user through association with this identifier. Note: It should be assumed that the current GPS location will be transmitted during UAS activation, which could reveal the true owner.
Do not connect personal social media accounts with devices used for University business. Disable any sharing of imagery or video with social media accounts.
Use a new mobile device without a SIM card installed or set up previously and never used for other activities for that will contain limited to no PII collectable by a foreign UAS company. For previously used devices, performing a wipe and factory reset of the mobile device prior to using it as a controller is advisable.
Periodically wipe or clear sensitive data from the system, including information stored on onboard or removable digital storage devices—such as SD and memory cards—and on connected flight controllers and mobile devices. Sensitive data should also be cleared before returning borrowed or rented UASs.
Avoid connecting the UAS to internal or private networks with sensitive data. Use a known secured network to register the UAS, and use a local backup device to store footage and data.
Before applying UAS patches and upgrades, consider their impact on operations.
Review user agreements to verify who has access to data collected by the UAS.
Inquire or review user agreements for information about third-party access to UAS data.
Maintain awareness of third-party collection and retention of data collected during UAS operations and develop appropriate policies to ensure the protection of intellectual property and sensitive operations.

title: New Tariffs on Drones
text:
The president decided to proclaim new tariffs on drones - link

New Section 232 tariffs on drones (UAS): Effective Sept 3, 2026, a 100% tariff applies to UAS over 25kg, thermal-imaging UAS, docking stations, and certain critical components (motors, batteries, controllers); a 25% tariff applies to UAS 25kg or under. A further 25% tariff on other listed UAS components takes effect Feb 9, 2027 (a 180-day delay meant to encourage domestic sourcing first).
Stated rationale: Commerce Dept investigation found the U.S. overly reliant on foreign UAS supply chains (even domestically-assembled drones use foreign parts), cited cybersecurity/data-exfiltration risks from foreign-made drone software, and concluded domestic manufacturing capacity is insufficient for military and civilian demand.
Carve-outs and incentives: Lower capped tariffs (15% or 10% for the UK) apply to Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, EU members, and the UK if components are certified as substantially originating there; companies with DoW/FCC-cleared products get a 180-day delay; and Commerce can grant tariff-free import allowances to companies committing to build new U.S. production facilities before January 2029, subject to monitoring and clawback for noncompliance or fraud.

title: New DETER Program
text:
The Drone Expedited and Targeted Enforcement Response (DETER) program supports the Administration’s Executive Order on Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty, which calls for stronger enforcement of drone laws to protect the safety and security of the U.S. airspace.
The program will support enhanced enforcement efforts around high-visibility events, including the upcoming FIFA World Cup matches from June 12 to July 19.
Under the DETER program:

Eligible first-time operators may resolve cases through reduced civil penalties or certificate suspensions.
Participants must admit liability and waive their right to appeal to receive expedited resolution.
Law enforcement partners will be able to notify the FAA of drone violations in real time.
The program is limited to less serious operational violations and will be implemented in select locations and timeframes.
The FAA will continue to handle violations involving significant safety risks, including unauthorized operations in restricted airspace, through standard enforcement procedures. These violations are not eligible for expedited resolution.

← Back to Recent News

title: NDAA 2026 - New Counter UAS Regulations
text:
The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for 2026 only had one major UAS related update. It created a new statutory carveout allowing state, local, and tribal law enforcement and correctional agencies to deploy counter-UAS technology under defined conditions, removing long-standing federal prohibitions that previously limited non-federal action.
Once certified, agencies are exempt from statutes such as the Wiretap Act and 18 U.S.C. Section 32, which otherwise prohibit interference with or destruction of aircraft in flight, when acting under this authority. Certified agencies may take actions deemed necessary to mitigate a credible threat posed by an unmanned aircraft system to:

Public safety
Facilities and assets
Large-scale public events and venues
Critical infrastructure
Correctional facilities

To qualify for this authority, agencies must:

Receive counter-UAS training from the Department of Homeland Security
Use counter-UAS systems approved by DHS and the Department of Defense
DHS and DoD have six months to issue implementing regulations, establish the training program, and define the equipment approval process.

title: Insurance
text:
The University of California has purchased an Unmanned Aircraft System Liability Policy. This policy has a total of $5 Mil limit including Personal Injury.
Coverage is automatic for UAS activity that meet the following criteria:

Flight operations are conducted on behalf and sanctioned by the University of California.
Aircraft weight under 55 lbs (at time of takeoff)
Flight operations are within Visual Line of Sight
Flight operations are below 400 ft above ground level.
Flight operations must be conducted within the United States.

Any UAS activity that do not meet the above criteria or operate outside the above criteria must be reported to and approved by the insurance underwriter in order to be covered.


The University of California has extended their UAS liability policy to enable coverage of UAS owned by UC students, staff or faculty used for University Business, including research. Coverage is contingent on compliance with the policy and procedures on UAS usage. This coverage is not intended to cover student organizations or 3rd Party vendors or contractors.



The University of California has extended their UAS liability policy to enable coverage of UAS by Campus Police. All coverage is contingent on the UAS activity being sanctioned by the UC.
Any UAS activity that is not approved by a Designated Local Authority or Systemwide Designated UAS Authority is not covered by this liability insurance.

title: Insurance
text:
Physical Damage Coverage
Physical damage to Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) registered with the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety is provided by a physical damage policy from the University’s captive insurance company, Fiat Lux Risk and Insurance Company.

Coverage applies in flight only when an approved flight plan is filed in accordance with UC UAS Policy, which includes the UC Drone web app or other means of compliance.
Coverage applies to Unmanned Aircraft Systems not in flight, but only if the Unmanned Aircraft Systems are registered with the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety at the time of the loss.
The policy limit per occurrence is $100,000 for UAS. Policy conditions and the scheduled value of the Unmanned Aircraft System may limit recovery. Unmanned Aircraft Systems are covered at present value not replacement cost. Depreciation does apply to claims for Unmanned Aircraft Systems.
Unmanned Aircraft Systems with values greater than $100,000 can be endorsed to the policy.
The UAS Physical Damage policy does not cover damage to payload or cargo; submit payload/cargo losses to the UC’s property policy.
A $1,000 deductible applies per loss. If an Unmanned Aircraft System loss results in damage to payload/cargo, the deductible is pro-rated between the policies.
In the event of a loss, please report to campus risk management.

This physical damage coverage does not extend to personally owned Unmanned Aircraft Systems used for University Business. Only Unmanned Aircraft Systems owned by the University of California are covered.

Filing a Claim
To file a claim, contact your campus Risk Manager. Please prepare the following:

Copy of the post-flight report (through UC Drones or other means of compliance)
Photographs of damaged equipment
Copy of original purchase invoice
Copy of invoice to ship the equipment back the manufacturer
Copy of repair invoice, if repairable
Copy of replacement quote, if not repairable

Ensure your coverage

Attach a copy of your UAS invoice to your UAS registration in UC Drones
Make sure you file your Flight Requests
For recurrent or on-going activity, create a Project application but don’t forget to add flights before you head out.
After an incident, make sure you take pictures of the damage and file a post-flight report. Add as much detail as possible.

title: Insurance
text:
3rd Party Insurance Minimum
All 3rd Party UAS activity, including on behalf of the University or other users of campus space, must have liability insurance with a preferred limit of $5 Mil. In addition to the limit that is provided by the Operator, a certificate of insurance along with a copy of the endorsement listing the following insurance clauses should be issued prior to commencement of services:

Name The University and its directors, officers, employees, servants and agents (collectively, the “Indemnified Parties” and individually, the “Indemnified Party”) as additional insureds, as their respective interests may appear
The Operator’s insurance shall be primary without any right of contribution from any other insurance available to The University
Include a cross liability or severability of interests among Indemnified Parties, providing that the insurance shall operate in all respects as if a separate policy had been issued covering each party insured
Include a waiver of subrogation in favor of the Indemnified Parties.
The certificate of insurance shall also provide that, in the event of a cancellation or material restrictive change of the policy which would adversely affect the interest of the Indemnified Parties, the insurers agree to provide 30 days prior written notice to The University.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
For any activity hosted by the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety, we expect participants to follow these rules. This includes any in-person training, virtual events, online forums and participation on social media.
The UC Center of Excellence is dedicated to providing a harassment-free experience for everyone whether in physical or virtual spaces. We do not tolerate harassment of community members or event participants in any form. Participants violating these rules may be sanctioned or expelled from the event at the discretion of the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety and any event organizers.
Harassment includes offensive verbal comments related to gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, group status, physical appearance, body size, race, or religion. In addition, harassment includes the acts of deliberate intimidation, stalking, following, unwelcome photography or recording, sustained disruption of talks or other events, inappropriate physical contact, and unwelcome sexual attention. Participants asked to stop any harassing behavior are expected to comply immediately.
If an event participant engages in harassing behavior, the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety or event organizers may take any action they deem appropriate, including warning the offender or expulsion from the event.
If you are being harassed, notice that someone else is being harassed, or have any other concerns, please contact us by email at UASsafety@ucmerced.edu. We will work with anyone who reports an issue and will work quickly to address the problem.

title: Mission
text:
The University of California Center of Excellence on Unmanned Aircraft System Safety provides system-wide expertise, support, and training for regulatory compliance, risk management, and the safe operation of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), commonly known as drones, across the University of California system. This covers all 10 UC campuses, UC Medical Centers, the Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources, the UC Natural Reserve System, UC Cooperative Extensions, and wherever UC conducts official business worldwide.
Since March 2016, the Center of UAS Safety has worked to develop effective safety and risk management strategies applicable to the wide variety of unmanned aircraft use and development in the UC system. Across the UC system, there are currently an estimated 300 active unmanned aircraft used by UC faculty, staff and students, and the number is growing daily. The UC UAS Policy was finalized in February 2018 to establish a standardized top-down management approach and to assign roles & responsibilities for oversight.

title: Mission
section: Regulatory Compliance, Risk Management and Training
text:
Regulatory Compliance, Risk Management and Training
The Center is focused on the following goals: - Promote UAS Safety through the development of a UAS Safety Management System, a four-pillared approach of Safety Policy, Safety Risk Management, Safety Assurance, and Safety Promotion - Develop effective UAS policies that define the processes and organization structure for UAS operations - Systematic processes for assessing and managing UAS risk - Fleet management system to provide continued monitoring of UAS activity and risk - Communicate UAS regulations and provide training
The wide range of UAS activity by UC affiliates and visitors necessitates a holistic approach to safety. The four-pillared approach, encapsulated as the UAS Safety Management System, structures safety as a combination of multiple aspects. This systematic approach is the first to manage UAS activity at the size and magnitude of the University of California system. While other agencies consider unmanned aircraft an isolated risk, the University of California has incorporated UAS into its Enterprise Risk Management approach.

title: Policy and FAQs
text:
The University of California recognizes that UAS offer great potential as tools for research and other educational functions as well as providing opportunities for recreational use and business pursuits across a diverse array of users and industries. The University also has an obligation to consider public safety, privacy, civil rights and civil liberties issues related to the use of UAS. In short, all UAS usage on UC property, for UC business or by UC-owned UAS must be pre-approved and documented by the designated UAS campus point of contact. In addition, non-UC operators on UC property must maintain sufficient liability insurance coverage.

title: Policy and FAQs
text:
Policy Frequently Asked Questions

Who do I contact to fly on my campus?
A list of the campus points of contact can be found here. Please understand that in many cases, the use of UAS on UC property are regulated by existing campus policies on activities, registered organizations and use of properties. These regulations are designed to protect and promote the rights of the members of the University, prevent interference with University functions or activities and assure compliance with all pertinent laws and other applicable University policies. For UC students, staff and faculty, you may submit a Flight Request with UC Drones Web App or contact the campus for additional or alternative means to submit a request.
I need to fly a drone for my research. What do I need to do? How long does it take for approval?
There may be several special circumstances, but in general, the operator must have an sUAS license from the FAA and must submit a Flight Request to the local campus point of contact. Depending on the complexity and timing of the request, the flight request could be approved in minutes or may take several weeks if extra FAA approval or coordination is necessary. A Flight Request may be a single flight, a set of flights or cover a year’s worth of activity – the details can be coordinated during the request.
What are the laws for flying a drone in the US?
The most common applicable set of laws for flying a drone is Part 107 (Flying for Work or Business https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/). This set of law requires the operator to have an SUAS license, have a registered drone and follow the drone laws that limit drone flying to up to 400 ft AGL, during daylight only and may not fly over people or moving vehicles. There are additionally special circumstances or restrictions for foreign nationals (international students, visiting scholars), operating on certain public lands, or within certain states or municipalities.
Can I fly a personal drone for my research project or my department?
Yes, as long as you comply with UC policy. Anyone operating under UC policy for university business (regardless of ownership) may additionally be provided with UC UAS liability insurance coverage free of charge.
I have a complicated or non-standard scenario. Who should I contact to identify what I need to do?
Please feel free to contact either your campus point of contact or the UC Center of Excellence on UAS Safety. We will work to ensure that there is a path forward for you to conduct your flight activity. We have experience with international UAS regulations, public agency airworthiness certification, night-time operations, airspace authorizations, DOT foreign national operator permits and agricultural spraying certificates to name a few.
I’m looking to fly a drone, but it says we are within 5 miles from the Davis Airport (KEDU). Is there anything we need to do to get approval to fly?
The Davis Airport (KEDU) is an airport in Class G airspace, and no Airspace Authorization is required. Additionally, the requirement to notify all airports within 5 miles has been rescinded. You may fly a drone wherever you have permission to do so, without being required to notify KEDU.

title: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking - BVLOS
text:
The FAA finally released their proposed regulations for BVLOS - https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/beyond-visual-line-sight-bvlos
The regulations are a little different than what was expected, but could be a good step forward.
Some notable items:

Part 108 is designed around Organizational management and oversight rather than individual pilot operations. The University of California would be the Operator (permit/certificate holder) for Part 108.

The ‘Operator’ in the regulations refer to the owner/management rather than the individual pilot. It’s a relic of older terminology, like how a ‘Person’ is defined as an individual, firm, company, or governmental entity (14 CFR 1.1). Think ‘Operator’ like Delta Airlines is an Operator.
Designation of Operations Supervisor (expected to be comparable to a Director of Aviation Operations)
Designation of Flight Coordinators (expected to have more direct involvement in flight operations, like a RPIC)
Both positions exempt from FAA licensing or individual certifications
Significant recordkeeping and reporting requirements

Part 108 has two options: Permits and Certificates. Both have specific purpose types, each with their own specific restrictions.

Operating Permits are the smaller in scale and scope. There are eight defined permit types:

Package Delivery
Agriculture (Spraying)
Aerial Surveying
Civit Interest (Law Enforcement/Emergency Response)
UAS Training
Demonstration
Recreational
Flight Test

Operating Certificates have steeper requirements but are less limiting. There are four defined certificate types:

Package Delivery
Agirculture (Spraying)
Aerial Surveying
Civic Interest (Law Enforcement/Emergency Response)

Operators may only have one of each type of Permit or Certificate. While most permits have limits on how many drones can be operated under each type (example: An Agriculture Permit only allows a fleet of 10), there are no fleet limits on certificates.

Aircraft operating under Part 108 are not limited by Part 107 restrictions. Part 108 allows drones up to 1,320 lbs, concurrent flight operations, and may operate over people.
Land zone restrictions and requirements based on population density. The FAA proposes to use LandScan as a source for population density, and drafted 5 Categories. For example, flight operations in Category 1 must be at least 50 ft away from any non-participant, while operations in Category 3 must not utilize unlicensed radio bands and are required to have an approved method of in-flight deconfliction. Different permit types also have limits on what Category zones they can operate over, for example, operations with an Aerial Surveying permit may only be allowed over people up to Category 3 zones. All UC campuses are in Category 4 zones.

Quick map of the daytime zones in California ArcGIS Online Map
Flight operations over open-air assemblies would still be prohibited regardless of the land Category.

The aircraft manufacturer is responsible for obtaining FAA authorization for Airworthiness Acceptance under Part 108. Only manufacturers within the US or a country with which the US has a Bilateral Airworthiness Agreement in place. There are significant manufacturing requirements, so it’s likely only the major manufacturers would want to go through these lengths.

Drones must be able to yield right of way to all aircraft broadcasting their position via ADS-B, necessitating some level of aircraft and object detection system either on-board or through other ground systems.

Operators may also utilize Automated Data Service Providers to provide real-time intelligence to the drone regarding weather and other air traffic.

We’ll continue to track how this rulemaking progresses. Public comments to the legislation will be posted here FAA Rulemaking Docket

title: FCC Announces Ban on Foreign-Made Drones
text:
In an unprecedented move, on December 22, 2025, the FCC declared that UAS and UAS critical component parts that are produced in foreign countries pose unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States and to the safety and security of U.S. persons, and should be included on the FCC’s Covered List.

FCC Press Release and Fact Sheet here
The updated FCC Covered List can be found here







ImportantRestrictions on foreign-made drones



New foreign-made drones are prohibited from receiving FCC authorization and are therefore prohibited from being imported for use or sale in the U.S. This update to the Covered List does not prohibit the import, sale, or use of any existing device models the FCC previously authorized.


This FCC action goes above and beyond the initial Section 1709 review that previously only targeted DJI and Autel. The final rule covers all foreign drones and components - not just those made in China, but all foreign countries including Canada, Switzerland, UK, and Germany. In addition, the updated definition for critical components now includes batteries and motors, in addition to the usual autopilots, controllers, and cameras.

title: FCC Proposes to Ban Import, Marketing of ‘Military’ Drones
text:
The FCC recently announced that they were proposing to remove FCC authorization to sell or market what they deem to be ‘military’ drones. Military drones in their definition includes drones over 55 lbs, drones with a LIDAR unit, and drones with a thermal imager. While certain DJI drones have been grandfathered in with existing FCC authorizations, this would remove them from being able to be sold in the US. The proposal would not ban their use - yet.
As an example, the DJI Matrice 4E received its FCC authorization before the ban, but if this new proposal is enacted, the FCC would remove its authorization to be sold in the US.
Comments to the FCC are due Sept 2, 2026

title: Counter UAS
text: The Department of Homeland Security has increasingly been issuing concerns over the potential of malicious drone use. Below are some guidance and resources for review:

title: Counter UAS
text:
UAS Threat Best Practices

Incorporate UAS into risk assessments. Assess critical assets and areas that may be most vulnerable to UAS. Identify and monitor possible launch and landing zones on or near facilities.
Establish procedures for safely handling downed UAS. Ensure that any downed UAS are rendered safe and properly handled to prevent potential harm to personnel, disruption of operations, or destruction of evidence.
Reevaluate security postures and security cameras and views to consider airborne threats.
Train employees on recognizing and reporting suspicious UAS activity.
Place ‘No Drone Zones’ signs in areas where UAS takeoff or landing is restricted.
Conduct exercises to test and prepare response capabilities should a UAS incident occur.
Update emergency action plans to include UAS incidents and responses. These might address evacuation protocols, depending on the model; visible hazardous attachments; or UAS payload size.
Consider using UAS detection technology and Remote ID receivers to enhance situational awareness of UAS activity. Consult legal counsel before employing detection technology, as certain systems may violate federal statutes and regulations.

title: Definitions
text: Common terms and acronyms used throughout this site and in UAS operations generally.

title: Definitions
text:
General

sUAS (Small Unmanned Aircraft System)

An unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 lbs (25 kg), the FAA’s regulatory category for most drones.

Part 107

The FAA regulation (14 CFR Part 107) governing most commercial and institutional small UAS operations in the United States.

Remote Pilot Certificate

The FAA certification required to operate a UAS under Part 107.

TRUST Certificate

The Recreational UAS Safety Test Certification for recreational, hobbyist, and many educational UAS operations.

VLOS (Visual Line of Sight)

The pilot or a visual observer must be able to see the aircraft, unaided except for corrective lenses, at all times during flight.

BVLOS (Beyond Visual Line of Sight)

Operations conducted outside the pilot’s unaided visual range. Requires a waiver or Certificate of Authorization under current regulations.

LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability)

The system used to request near-real-time airspace authorization in controlled airspace.

TFR (Temporary Flight Restriction)

A short-term airspace restriction, often issued for wildfires, VIP movement, or large events.

NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions)

An official notice containing information relevant to flight safety, including airspace restrictions.

title: Definitions
text:
Operational

PIC (Pilot in Command)

The individual with final responsibility for a UAS operation, whether or not they are manipulating the controls directly.

VO (Visual Observer)

A person assisting the PIC by maintaining visual contact with the aircraft, allowing the PIC to attend to other mission-critical tasks.

GCS (Ground Control Station)

The equipment used to monitor and, where applicable, control a UAS during flight.

title: Definitions
text:
Technical & Equipment

MTOW (Maximum Takeoff Weight)

An approximation of a drone’s relative size and regulatory category.

RTK (Real-Time Kinematic)

A GNSS correction technique providing centimeter-level positioning accuracy in real time, used for precision mapping.

PPK (Post-Processed Kinematic)

Similar to RTK, but positioning corrections are applied after the flight rather than in real time.

GSD (Ground Sample Distance)

The real-world size represented by a single pixel in captured imagery; a key measure of mapping resolution.

Gimbal

A motorized stabilization mount that keeps a camera steady independent of the aircraft’s movement.

VTOL (Vertical Takeoff and Landing)

Describes aircraft capable of taking off and landing vertically, including some fixed-wing mapping drones.

FPV (First Person View)

Flight controlled via a live video feed from the aircraft’s perspective, rather than by direct visual observation.

Multispectral Sensor

A camera capturing multiple specific light wavelength bands (e.g., red, green, near-infrared) beyond standard visible-light photography, commonly used in agricultural and research imaging.

Thermal Sensor

A camera capturing infrared radiation to visualize heat differences, used in inspection, wildlife monitoring, and search operations.

title: Definitions
text:
Regulations

COA (Certificate of Waiver or Authorization)

An FAA approval permitting a public operator (including public universities) to conduct specific UAS operations, such as BVLOS, that would otherwise be prohibited.

Remote ID

The requirement for most drones to broadcast identification and location information in flight, comparable to a digital license plate.

FRIA (FAA-Recognized Identification Area)

A defined location where drones may be flown without Remote ID equipment.

NDAA / Section 848

The National Defense Authorization Act; Section 848 refers to specific UAS-related provisions restricting the use of federal funds for certain foreign-manufactured drones. See NDAA Compliance.

Blue UAS

A Department of Defense-cleared list of drones approved for federal use. See the Blue UAS Cleared List.

Domestic End Product

The Buy American Standard test for whether an article qualifies as domestically manufactured, based on U.S. assembly and a domestic-component cost threshold. Full regulatory text (48 C.F.R. § 25.101)

UAS Critical Components

Components, including software, the FCC defines as core to a UAS for Covered List purposes: flight controllers, navigation systems, sensors, batteries, motors, and more. FCC drone/UAS Covered List page

Toy Drone

An FCC-defined exemption category for very small, sensor-free, non-connected recreational drones meeting twelve specific criteria. FCC drone/UAS Covered List page

Military-Grade UAS (proposed)

A proposed FCC definition covering heavier, sensor-equipped, or swarm-capable UAS. DA-26-758

Power Inverters

Foreign-produced bi-directional power conversion devices with remote connectivity, added to the FCC Covered List in 2026. DA-26-786

Advanced Robotic Devices

Foreign-produced mobile robots (including humanoids and quadrupeds) meeting specific weight, sensor, and connectivity criteria, added to the FCC Covered List in 2026. DA-26-786

title: Operations Over People
text: In April 2021, the FAA updated Part 107 regulations for operations over people. Eligibility depends on both the aircraft’s certification category and the type of Remote ID compliance in use.

title: Operations Over People
text:
Category Levels

Category 0 — Not Eligible for Flights Over People. The aircraft does not meet the requirements of any category below. Under the baseline Part 107 rule, it may only be flown over a person who is directly participating in the operation, located under a covered structure, or inside a stationary vehicle. “Cat 0” is not an FAA term; it is used on this page to label aircraft that fall outside the four official categories.
Category 1 — Under 250 g including payload, with rotor protections. The lowest-risk category. If the aircraft weighs 0.55 lb or less at takeoff, including any attached payload, and has no exposed rotating parts capable of lacerating skin, it qualifies automatically, with no FAA declaration required.
Category 2 — FAA-certified, under 11 ft-lb kinetic energy, with rotor protections. The aircraft (or aircraft-and-accessory combination) must be certified, through an FAA-accepted means of compliance, not to cause an injury more severe than the transfer of 11 foot-pounds of kinetic energy on impact with a rigid object.
Category 3 — FAA-certified, under 25 ft-lb kinetic energy, with rotor protections. Same certification approach as Category 2, at a higher kinetic-energy threshold. Category 3 aircraft carry additional operating limits: they may not fly over open-air assemblies of people, and are limited to access-controlled sites or brief, transient flights over individuals.
Category 4 — FAA airworthiness certificate under Part 21. The most demanding category, requiring a manned-aircraft-style airworthiness certificate rather than a declared means of compliance. This category is generally not applicable to typical Part 107 operations.

title: Operations Over People

title: Remote Identification
text:
Remote ID is a system that broadcasts a drone’s identity, location, and flight information while it is in the air, comparable to a digital license plate. The broadcast can be received by anyone with a compatible receiver, allowing nearby individuals and law enforcement to identify aircraft in the airspace.
For more information about Remote Identification, please visit the FAA’s website here

title: Remote Identification
text:
Ways to Comply
A drone must meet Remote ID requirements in one of three ways.

Standard Remote Identification
Most drones manufactured after December 2022 have RID already built-in to the drone’s firmware. Standard RID displays the drone’s location, altitude and speed, as well as the location and altitude of it’s operation station.


Broadcast Remote Identification
For drones that don’t have RemoteID built in, pilots must install a Remote ID broadcast module. This is a a small and lightweight component that can be added externally to a drone. It functions the same as standard remote identification, minus the ability to broadcast the location of the drone’s operator. Modules can only display the location of the drone’s takeoff point. Examples include the BlueMark DroneBeacon db120, the Dronetag Beacon, and the Spektrum SkyID (for RC aircraft).



DroneTag Beacon




FAA Recognized Identification Area (FRIA)
For drones that do not have RID capabilities, the FAA is allowing pilots to fly their drones only in FAA Recognized Identification Areas. As of now, only Educational institutions and FAA-recognized Community Based Organizations can apply for a FRIA.
The Drone Map of California has been updated with all approved FRIAs in California: Drone Map of California.

title: Remote Identification
text:
Updating your Registration
To complete the transition to Remote ID, all drone registrations must be updated on the FAA Drone Zone.

Log into FAA Drone Zone
From your dashboard, enter your drone inventory.

Find the drone registration you want to update, and click the three vertical dots to open the menu.

Select ‘Edit’ from the dropdown menu.

In the new window, when it asks ‘Does your drone broadcast FAA Remote ID information?’ select ‘YES.’
Update your UAS TYPE - the options will change when you select ‘YES’

Select either ‘Standard Remote ID’ or ‘Remote ID Broadcast Module’

Enter in the Remote ID Serial Number

If your drone has Remote ID built-in (ie, Standard Remote ID), use your drone’s serial number.
If you are adding a Remote ID Broadcast Module, use the Remote ID Broadcast Module’s serial number.

title: Remote Identification
text:
Frequently Asked Questions
Is compliance mandatory? Yes. Remote ID is required by federal regulation and enforced by the FAA. Failure to comply is a violation of University policy and may result in disciplinary action.
Should I choose a Standard Remote ID drone or a broadcast module? Standard Remote ID is simpler and does not carry the added visual-line-of-sight condition that applies to broadcast modules. A module is a practical option for an existing drone that lacks built-in capability.
After installing a module, is further configuration required? Within the US, typically not, beyond updating the registration. Additional configuration may be needed if the drone will be used internationally.
How do I read Remote ID broadcasts? See Reading Remote ID.

title: The EASA formula
text: The dashed black curve in the VLOS estimator comes from guidance published by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). It is the only widely published formula that turns a drone’s size into a VLOS distance, which makes it a useful reference point for the acuity model.
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

title: The EASA formula
text:
The formula
EASA’s Guidelines for UAS operations in the open and specific category (Issue 03, 17 July 2025) compute VLOS from two parameters and use the smaller one.
Attitude line of sight (ALOS) is the farthest distance at which the pilot can still see the drone’s position and orientation, based on its size:
\[
\text{ALOS}_{\text{multirotor}} = 327 \times CD + 20\ \text{m}
\qquad
\text{ALOS}_{\text{fixed-wing}} = 490 \times CD + 30\ \text{m}
\]
\(CD\) is the characteristic dimension in meters, which EASA defines as the drone’s maximum dimension. For a multirotor that is usually the prop-tip-to-prop-tip distance; for a fixed-wing it is usually the wingspan.
Detection line of sight (DLOS) is the distance within which the pilot can spot other aircraft in time to avoid them:
\[
\text{DLOS} = 0.3 \times GV
\]
\(GV\) is ground visibility. EASA recommends at least 5 km, which gives a DLOS of 1,500 m (about 4,920 ft).
\[
\text{VLOS} = \min(\text{ALOS},\ \text{DLOS})
\]
EASA’s guidelines credit additional detail to a guidance document from Germany’s Federal Aviation Office (LBA). They also state that the guidelines are not legally binding.






NoteWhat the estimator shows



The estimator plots ALOS only. For the drones on this page, ALOS is far below a 5 km DLOS, so DLOS would not change the result in good visibility. In poor visibility it can: at 1 km ground visibility, DLOS drops to 300 m (about 984 ft).
crumbs: How far can you really see the drone?

title: The EASA formula
text:
Straight-line vs. horizontal distance
EASA measures VLOS as the straight-line distance between the pilot and the drone. The estimator’s x-axis is horizontal distance, so the ALOS limit is converted at each altitude \(a\):
\[
d_{\text{horizontal}} = \sqrt{\text{ALOS}^2 - a^2}
\]
That is why the dashed curve bends toward the y-axis as altitude increases. Drawing it as a vertical line would overstate how far the drone can go horizontally at altitude.

title: The EASA formula
text:
How this compares to Part 107
US rules don’t set a VLOS distance. 14 CFR 107.31 instead requires the pilot or visual observer to see the drone well enough to:

know its location;
determine its attitude, altitude, and direction of flight;
observe the airspace for other traffic or hazards; and
determine that it does not endanger people or property.

EASA’s two parameters map loosely onto these abilities. ALOS relates to item 2 (seeing attitude), and DLOS relates to item 3 (seeing other traffic). This is an interpretation for comparison, not an FAA position. Part 107 also sets a minimum flight visibility of 3 statute miles (about 4.8 km) in 14 CFR 107.51.

title: How far can you really see the drone?
text:
Introduction
Maintaining visual line of sight (VLOS) of a drone is a fundamental requirement under 14 CFR Part 107, which governs the commercial use of small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) in the United States. According to these regulations, drone pilots (or their visual observers) must always be able to see their aircraft unaided by any device other than corrective lenses.
In practical terms, “visual line of sight” means that the operator or observer can clearly identify the drone’s orientation and location in real time. While this may sound straightforward, factors such as distance, weather conditions, obstacles, and lighting can all compromise VLOS. Consequently, ensuring VLOS compliance across varying operational scenarios is not always a simple task.
Despite its importance, relatively little research has been dedicated to developing systematic methods to estimate or verify VLOS. Most current industry practices rely on manual observation and conservative flight planning to ensure the drone remains within sight, but these approaches can be subjective and prone to human error.
